Machine class: macOS 26.3.0, arm64, 10 CPUs, .NET 10.0.14, workstation concurrent GC (serverGC=False), no GC env overrides. All 3 tests passed in 7.2 min. MB is 10^6 bytes; cells are data rows x columns; growth is peak working set minus a 1 MiB-stream baseline of the same shape; the ceiling is MemoryBudget.CeilingBytes for the pass.
PLAIN 12 columns, 1 GiB (10,737,418 rows, 128.8M cells; ASSERTED): read only 0.87 s (1229 MB/s); byte pass 1.75 s (615 MB/s), growth 1.1 MB vs ceiling 67.1 MB; full profile 84.1 s (12.8 MB/s, 1.53 Mcells/s), peak 79.3 MB, growth 7.1 MB vs ceiling 76.5 MB (estimate 9.4 MB).

Per byte the full profile is similar for plain and padded (12.8 and 15.0 MB/s); per cell the wide shape is about 6.6 times slower, so at this size cost tracks bytes more than cells.
RECOMMENDATION (the owner decides): keep the three passes for 1.0.0. Fusing the byte pass into another pass could save at most about 3 percent. The benchmark did not time the scoring pass and the delimited pass separately, so it cannot say what fusing those two would gain; if the owner wants that decision, file an item to time them separately first.

items.title: First-record ceiling for byte-limited profiling

note_records.text:
**2026-10-28** — OPEN QUESTIONS for the owner (not decided; the failing tests marked pending depend on them).
Q1. Outcome when the first record is longer than N. (a) SqualifyException with a clear message, nothing profiled: simplest, a consumer that wants a refusal gets one, but the CLI and library produce no descriptor. (b) An issue code (e.g. firstRecordTooLong) with scope.complete false and an empty or partial profile: the descriptor stays a result, but sq-35 decided "never an empty profile for a file with data", so this needs a partial profile of the first N+1 bytes or an explicit exception to that rule, and the cap must then be written in scope to keep descriptors self-describing and deterministic. Also decide the CLI exit code.
Q2. Does the ceiling also apply without --max-bytes? (a) Yes: it caps the first record of a whole-file profile, which then fails early on a file with no line breaks. (b) No, rejected without --max-bytes: keeps it a byte-limit companion; a whole-file run has no overshoot to bound. Note: the whole-file path never calls ScopeCut today, so (a) adds a new early read of the first record before the byte pass.
Q3. Interaction with the cuts. Proposed reading, to confirm: N counts bytes of the first record including its terminator in the charset code units (CRLF counts 2, UTF-16 terminator 2, UTF-32 4); a bare CR as byte N needs one more unit to see whether an LF follows, so reading N+1 bytes (or one unit more) is allowed for that lookahead and the record is then N+1 if it is CRLF; for UTF-16/32 stop at the first whole unit past N rather than at exactly N+1 bytes; a binary file (cut exactly at the limit, no records) is not subject. Also: does N below --max-bytes make the check run before the window sniff (the test list assumes yes)?

**2026-10-28** — Owner decisions (2026-10-28), verbatim: Q1 outcome "SqualifyException (Recommended)" (option text: "Fail with a clear message, nothing profiled; the CLI exits non-zero with the message. Simplest, and matches a consumer that wants to refuse the file. No descriptor member or issue code is added, so the schema is untouched before the freeze."). Q2 "Reject it without --max-bytes (Recommended)" (option text: "It is a companion of the byte limit. A whole-file run has no first-record overshoot to bound, and the whole-file path never goes through ScopeCut today, so this adds no new early read."). Q3 "Accept as proposed (Recommended)" (proposal: N counts bytes of the first record including its terminator in the charset code units (CRLF = 2, UTF-16 unit = 2, UTF-32 = 4); a bare CR as byte N reads one more unit to see whether an LF follows (the record is N+1 if it is CRLF); UTF-16/32 stop at the first whole unit past N; binary files (cut exactly at the limit, no records) are not subject; the check runs before the window sniff when N is below --max-bytes).

**2026-10-28** — Verified outcome: MaxFirstRecordBytes / --max-first-record-bytes added. items.title: Shared prefix reading

note_records.text:
**2026-10-28** — OPEN QUESTIONS for the owner (not decided; the failing tests marked pending depend on them).
Q4. API shape. (a) Profiler.ProfilePrefix(source, options) returning (Descriptor, ReadOnlyMemory<byte> prefix, scope): one call, the guarantee that the descriptor describes the bytes holds by construction, reads from an IProfileSource so file.size comes from source.Length. (b) Public PrefixReader.Read(stream, maxBytes, maxFirstRecordBytes): reusable without profiling, but then the consumer must feed the bytes back to Profiler, and the guarantee and the single read are lost unless the reader also hands over the source; a stream of unknown length gives no whole-file size. (c) Both, with ProfilePrefix built on PrefixReader: larger public surface to keep stable. Also the return type: a tuple, or a named record (ProfiledPrefix) that can grow.
Q5. Memory. The prefix is buffered up to maxBytes plus the overshoot (a CRLF unit, or the rest of a long first line). With item sq-39 the overshoot is bounded by N; without it a file with no line breaks is buffered whole. Options: (a) accept and document the bound as maxBytes + overshoot, with sq-39 as the way to cap it; (b) require MaxBytes (and possibly MaxFirstRecordBytes) for this API and reject null; (c) add a hard internal ceiling on the buffer. Also: does the API accept MaxBytes null (whole file buffered)?
Q6. Is the cut rule a documented contract consumers may rely on? Today design.md describes it but the user guide only says "cut at a whole line". Making it a contract (in descriptor.md or the user guide) means any change to it is a breaking change needing a descriptor or API version note; leaving it undocumented means the consumer relies on the guarantee "same bytes as scope.bytesRead" only. Contract text would cover: binary cut at the limit; text cut after the last LF, CR or CRLF in the charset code units inside the limit; a CR ending the window takes the LF after it; no terminator inside the limit reads on to the first terminator or the end of the file.

**2026-10-28** — Owner decisions (2026-10-28), verbatim: Q4 API shape "Profiler.ProfilePrefix returning a record (Recommended)" (option text: "ProfilePrefix(source, options) returns a named record (descriptor, ReadOnlyMemory<byte> prefix, scope), not a bare tuple, so it can grow. One call; the descriptor describes the bytes by construction; one read; file.size from source.Length."). Q5 memory "Require MaxBytes; document the bound (Recommended)" (option text: "ProfilePrefix rejects a null MaxBytes (it would buffer the whole file). The buffer is at most MaxBytes plus the overshoot, and sq-39 MaxFirstRecordBytes is the documented way to cap the overshoot. No new hard ceiling."). Q6 cut rule "Yes, document it as a contract (Recommended)" (option text: "Document in the user guide: binary cut at the limit; text cut after the last LF, CR or CRLF in the charset code units inside the limit; a CR ending the window takes the LF after it; no terminator inside the limit reads on to the first terminator or the end. Any later change is a documented breaking change.").

Prism cuts its own 1 MiB prefix (PrefixBytes.Read) and refuses a header over 1 MiB itself; if it migrates to ProfilePrefix, its equality tests in SqualifyDescriberTests would catch a cut-rule divergence. Keep IProfileSource public and unchanged.

**2026-10-29** — Owner decisions (2026-10-29), verbatim, after the review: R2 "Never read past Length (Recommended)" (option text: "BufferedSource stops at the declared Length, so memory stays bounded and the descriptor still describes exactly Prefix. file.size is the reported Length, as documented. Bytes beyond Length are simply not part of the file as the source declares it."). R4 "Contract includes the window sniff (Recommended)" (option text: "Reword to a file whose bytes inside the limit sniff as binary / the charset sniffed from the bytes inside the limit, state that a limit shorter than a BOM can sniff differently, and that a sniff change that moves a cut is a documented breaking change. Keeps your Q6 decision.").

items.title: Count the distinct spellings in the other counters

note_records.text:
**2026-10-28** — OPEN QUESTIONS for the owner (not decided; the failing tests marked pending depend on them).
Q1. Exact, capped or approximate. SpellingCounter forgets a dropped spelling, so a distinct count needs it to remember something. (a) Exact: remember a hash (XxHash64, 8 bytes) of every distinct dropped spelling; exact up to hash collisions, but unbounded memory on a column with millions of distinct spellings. (b) Capped exact: remember up to K more (K to be set, for example 64 or 1,000), count past it as the cap and write a marker (a capped flag or an approximate flag as distinct, numeric and temporal use); bounded, but the consumer sees "at least K". (c) Sketch (HyperLogLog, deterministic, marked approximate with its relative error); bounded and fits the sq-38 budget, but small distinct counts (1 versus 2) are exact only in the linear-counting range, and 1 versus many is the use case here. For the stated use case ("is there a single spelling") any of the three answers 1 versus more than 1, so (b) with a small K may be enough.
Q2. Member names, omission and totals. Fields: nullSpellingsOtherDistinct, left out when 0 like nullSpellingsOther; rowClasses: allNullRowSpellingsOtherDistinct, always written like allNullRowSpellingsOther. Confirm, or name them differently. If Q1 is (b) or (c), also decide the marker member (nullSpellingsOtherDistinctCapped, or approximate).
Q3. What counts as distinct. Proposed: each distinct dropped spelling once, whether it was dropped by the 64 bound or by the 256-character bound, compared as exact text (not trimmed, as nullSpellings keys are). A spelling dropped by the 64 bound that also appears again counts once. Confirm.
Q4. Pass and ordering. Depends on sq-42 for the shared limits members; the pass is not set. If Q1 is (b) or (c), the cap or precision might also be published in limits (an sq-42 style member); decide whether to include it here.

**2026-10-29** — Owner decisions (2026-10-29), verbatim: Q1 "Capped exact count, marked capped (Recommended)" (option text: "Remember a hash (XxHash64) of up to K further distinct spellings (K small, for example 64), count exactly up to K, and write a marker when the cap is hit. Bounded memory, deterministic, and answers the use case (one spelling versus more than one) exactly."). Q2 "nullSpellingsOtherDistinct omitted at 0; allNullRowSpellingsOtherDistinct always written (Recommended)" (option text: "Mirrors nullSpellingsOther (left out when 0) and allNullRowSpellingsOther (always written). If the count is capped, a sibling marker member (for example nullSpellingsOtherDistinctCapped) is written only when the cap is hit."). Q3 "Accept as proposed, K = 64 (Recommended)" (proposal: each distinct dropped spelling counts once however often it recurs, whether dropped by the 64-spelling bound or by the 256-character bound, compared as exact text, not trimmed; exact up to K = 64 further distinct spellings; the capped marker is written once more were seen; option text: "Per field and for all-null rows the counter remembers at most 64 more spelling hashes (XxHash64, 8 bytes each, plus length for the long ones), so at most about 0.5 KiB more per spilling field; the marker is nullSpellingsOtherDistinctCapped (true only when the cap is hit)."). Q4 "Yes, publish it in limits.nullSpellings (Recommended)" (option text: "Same reasoning as sq-42: a consumer reads the cap instead of hard-coding it. sq-43 adds the third member to the object sq-42 creates (always written, per the sq-42 answer)."). What a patch release may change in the descriptor

goals:
- **Deterministic descriptor.** The same input bytes and the same squalify version give a byte-identical descriptor on every OS and CPU. No ML, LLM or network.
- **Full streaming scan with bounded memory.** Statistics are exact up to documented caps, then come from deterministic sketches that the descriptor marks as approximate.
- **v1 formats:** delimited text (preambles, annotation and units rows, repeated blocks) and a generic byte profile for binary files. Touchstone, whole-file key=value/INI documents and the STDF V4 walk with a test catalog follow as additive 1.x minor releases (sq-09, sq-10).
- **Useful for classification:** structural fingerprints (structure, layout, typed, names), layout regions, row classes, detect-rule hints, the header-unit convention, a `kind` label (byte-class interim label in 1.0; the fixed built-in rule set follows as a 1.x minor, sq-15), and an evidence trail for every inference.
- **Values are opt-in.** No literal data values without `--include-values`, or `--include-values-for` for named keys and columns. Header names, preamble keys, test names, and numeric and temporal statistics are always included, except for file-constant fields, whose statistics would reveal the value.
- **A stable, versioned descriptor schema** (docs/descriptor.md, frozen with a JSON Schema at v1).
- **Explained in plain language.** docs/how-it-works.md, with Mermaid diagrams, kept current at every architectural review.
non_goals:
- Proposing DataBall configs or file types. DataBall consumes descriptors in its own roadmap.
- Classifying files against a user library of known types. The built-in `kind` label is in scope.
- ML, LLM or network use.
- Editing, repairing or converting files.
- A dependency on DataBall. The descriptor schema is the contract.
- In v1: directory or multi-file input, decompression, STDF result values, and MIR text fields.
